name: Gastric sleeve

lead: Sleeve gastrectomy removes most of the stomach, leaving a narrow tube. It is a medical treatment for severe obesity and, according to Wikipedia, the most commonly performed bariatric operation worldwide. The appearance payoff people link to it is large fat loss, giving a leaner body and slimmer face.

Removing roughly three quarters or more of the stomach limits how much food can be eaten and removes the part that produces the appetite hormone ghrelin. Research also describes effects on gut hormones and glucose handling beyond weight loss alone. Systematic reviews report weight loss and resolution of conditions like type 2 diabetes comparable to gastric bypass. It is studied as a medical treatment, not a cosmetic one, and no studies on appearance outcomes were identified.

paras: It is usually done laparoscopically under general anaesthesia, with eligibility set by clinical guidelines based on body mass index and health conditions. Afterwards people follow staged diets and vitamin supplementation, and weight loss builds over many months.

Documented risks include staple-line leaks, bleeding, clots, infection, reflux, nausea and vomiting, vitamin and thiamine deficiencies (including rare Wernicke encephalopathy), gastric dilation, and weight regain that may lead to revision surgery. The operation is considered irreversible.

social.title: Ask HN: Hack my weight with a sleeve gastrectomy?

angle.text: A reduced stomach leads to large, sustained weight loss, which users link to a leaner body and slimmer face. It is studied for weight loss and diabetes in severe obesity, with documented surgical and nutritional risks.

lead: Sleeve gastrectomy, often called the gastric sleeve, is a bariatric operation usually performed laparoscopically in which roughly 75 to 85 percent of the stomach is removed along its greater curvature, leaving a narrow, banana-sized, tube-shaped stomach.[1] It is used to treat severe obesity and obesity-related conditions such as type 2 diabetes.[2][3]

Its link to appearance runs through weight loss: smaller stomach volume and removal of the ghrelin-producing part of the stomach reduce appetite and intake, patients commonly lose 50 to 70 percent of their excess weight, and a leaner body and face can follow.[1] In ascension and body-transformation circles the operation is sometimes discussed as the most extreme route to a slimmer frame, though it is a medical obesity treatment rather than a cosmetic one and carries surgical and nutritional risks.

Wikipedia describes it as having begun as a modification of the duodenal switch and as the first stage of a two-step operation in very high-risk patients before being used on its own, and as now the most commonly performed bariatric surgery worldwide.[1] Systematic reviews report weight loss and comorbidity resolution comparable to gastric bypass, along with risks such as staple-line leak.[3][4] No studies on appearance outcomes specifically were identified.
infobox: About 150 mL, calibrated over a bougie[1]
Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, adjustable gastric band, duodenal switch
Leak, reflux, nutritional deficiency, weight regain

paras: The surgeon makes a longitudinal resection of the stomach starting from the antrum about 5 to 6 cm from the pylorus and finishing near the cardia. The remaining stomach is calibrated over a tube called a bougie, usually 36 to 40 Fr, and the remaining stomach is roughly 150 mL.[1] A first-in-human trial tested a fluorescence-guided calibration tube during sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass, with 21 sleeve and 10 bypass procedures.[5] Variants include banded sleeve gastrectomy, which places a band to limit dilation of the sleeve.[6]

Weight loss comes from smaller stomach volume and from removal of the portion that produces ghrelin, the hormone that stimulates appetite.[1] Wikipedia also notes improvements in glucose handling before major weight loss has occurred, which it relates to reduced gastric volume, changes in gut peptides and expression of genes involved in glucose absorption.[1]

The operation was originally performed as a modification of the duodenal switch and later as the first part of a two-stage operation in extremely obese patients for whom gastric bypass was judged too risky; the initial weight loss was so good that it began to be studied as a stand-alone procedure.[1] A 2003 report described reoperative sleeve gastrectomy after failure of the duodenal switch,[7] a 2006 study asked whether gastric dilation limits the sleeve as a sole operation,[8] and a 2008 paper reviewed its indications as a primary procedure in the morbidly obese.[2] A combined liver transplantation and sleeve gastrectomy protocol for patients with obesity and end-stage liver disease was reported in 2013.[9]

A 2014 JAMA systematic review of long-term follow-up after bariatric surgery assessed weight loss and the course of type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidemia in severely obese adults and noted the limited number of long-term studies with good retention.[3]

Wikipedia reports typical excess-weight loss of 50-70% over two years and cites a 2021 Lancet meta-analysis of 174,772 participants linking bariatric surgery to a 59% reduction in all-cause mortality in obese adults with type 2 diabetes and 30% without.[1] Studies in non-morbidly obese patients with diabetes have examined effects on insulin secretion.[10] A 2022 meta-analysis found better weight loss at 3 and 5 years after banded versus non-banded sleeve gastrectomy with no difference in comorbidity outcomes.[6]

Reviews note that the metabolic effects of bariatric surgery appear to exceed what weight loss alone would explain, and that changes to gastric emptying alter glucose handling.[11][12] Wikipedia also describes use in children and adolescents, endorsed by the International Federation for the Surgery of Obesity and Metabolic Disorders and the American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery, with weight loss comparable to adults.[1]

Weight loss after the operation reduces body fat and changes body shape, and patients commonly describe visible changes in the face and body as weight comes off. No studies of appearance outcomes after sleeve gastrectomy were identified in the literature reviewed for this article, so appearance changes are not quantified here.
Reviews of nutritional outcomes note that rapid weight loss can accompany micronutrient deficiencies, which clinicians monitor after the sleeve.[13]

Large trials have compared the operation with others: a registered trial of sleeve gastrectomy versus gastric bypass enrolled 280 patients, one comparing gastric bypass, band and sleeve enrolled 1,351, and the BEST trial enrolled 1,752.[14][15][16] A trial in older patients compared sleeve and bypass.[17] Smaller randomized trials have examined analgesia after sleeve surgery, day-case discharge, omentopexy and gastric dilation, and anesthetic reversal.[18][19][20][21]
Observational work includes a review of gastric dilation after sleeve gastrectomy as a sole operation and a study of liraglutide for insufficient weight loss or regain after bariatric surgery.[8][22]

A systematic analysis of 4,888 patients examined staple-line leak, described as an ongoing concern, and a World Journal of Gastroenterology review covers its prevention and management.[4][23] Wikipedia lists leak (about 1 in 200 patients), blood clots (about 1%), wound infection (about 10 to 15%), strictures (about 3.5%), reflux, nausea, vitamin B12 deficiency, reduced bone health, depression and weight regain among complications.[1]

A review of 118 cases described Wernicke encephalopathy after bariatric surgery, including after sleeve procedures, and advised testing and treating thiamine deficiency.[24] Case reports describe gastric twist obstruction after laparoscopic sleeve.[25] The operation is irreversible, and revision surgery or drugs such as liraglutide are used when weight loss is insufficient or weight is regained.[22][7]
